arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Chief Justice Roberts opened the session and recognized Monsanto's counsel. Three lawyers argued: Clement for Monsanto, Harris for the United States supporting Monsanto, and Keller for the Missouri side.

Monsanto asked the Court to hold that FIFRA bars a state failure-to-warn claim demanding a cancer warning EPA did not require. It stressed that registrants cannot add warnings unilaterally; EPA approval is required.
The United States asked the Court to find express and impossibility preemption. It cited federal rules requiring adherence to the EPA-approved label and governing hazard statements.

The Missouri side asked the Court to allow the suit. Keller argued registration is no misbranding defense and misbranding is not limited to label-registration matching. He distinguished Riegel on statutory grounds and preserved parallel claims. Monsanto answered that a registered product sold with the approved label is not misbranded.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Monsanto sells a weed killer whose label the EPA approved. A Missouri lawsuit blamed the product for cancer and demanded a stronger warning. The dispute is whether federal pesticide law blocks that state suit.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The case reached the Supreme Court as No. 24-1068. Chief Justice Roberts opened the argument session and called on Monsanto's lawyer first. Paul Clement argued for Monsanto. Sarah Harris argued for the United States, backing Monsanto. Ashley Keller argued for the Missouri side.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 4, lines 11-21

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Monsanto asks the Court to rule that state law cannot force a cancer warning the EPA did not require. It says federal law overrides the state claim. It also says a company cannot add warnings alone; EPA approval comes first.

The United States agrees with Monsanto. It says Missouri demands a warning while federal rules require sticking to the EPA-approved label. Those two demands cannot both be obeyed, so federal law wins. EPA also requires data before label changes happen, so no company can rewrite warnings by itself. Prior cases call this impossibility preemption.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Monsanto's core position: a product registered with EPA and sold with the approved label is not misbranded. That answers the state's accusation directly.

The Missouri side answers the other way. Its lawyer says federal approval does not excuse misbranding, and misbranding reaches more than label-to-registration mismatches. He also distinguished an earlier drug case called Riegel. He said this law has no matching provision, no statutory label lock, and preserves parallel claims.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: One justice asked where the preemption comes from: the statute, regulations, or the labeling rule itself. That probes the foundation of Monsanto's argument.

Justice Kavanaugh asked whether deviating from the EPA-approved label would itself violate federal law. That tests whether the Missouri warning demand is even possible. He also pressed the Missouri side, saying differing state liability outcomes clash with national uniformity. Justice Kagan asked what uniformity the Missouri approach achieves under FIFRA's uniformity clause. That question cuts the other way.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The ruling could shape many pesticide lawsuits. If Monsanto wins, EPA-approved labels would shield companies from state warning claims. If the Missouri side wins, juries in different states could reach different results. The justices' questions show the tension. Uniformity favors one national rule. But FIFRA's own text and preserved state claims cut toward allowing some lawsuits.
